name: PT Sekar Bumi Tbk

frontmatter.title: Sekar Bumi: a duty gross-up hiding a real spread
frontmatter.summary: A value-added shrimp exporter whose reported margin is inflated by a US trade-duty charge that runs through both revenue and selling expenses. Nine-month FY2026 accounts show the ex-duty spread holding near its FY2025 peak, the duty still rising, and the shares below book at a mid-single-digit multiple of our FY2026E EBITDA, with a possible refund the market does not price. We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp739, 62.4% total return.
thesis: The duty line is a pass-through gross-up, not a margin tax: duties rose from IDR54.9bn in FY2024 to IDR312.6bn in FY2025 and to IDR360.1bn in 9M2026, and the LK says the tariff was passed to customers and the selling price accounted for duties [S3][S4]. It therefore inflates revenue and selling expense together, which is why the reported gross margin is not comparable across years.
The recovery is already in the accounts, not in our forecast: nine-month FY2026 sales were IDR2,811.9bn with gross profit of IDR732.9bn and net profit of IDR120.2bn [S4].
On an ex-duty basis the product spread widened from the FY2024 trough to a FY2025 peak and held in 9M2026 — a real recovery from the trough that does not depend on the duty falling [S4][S5].

At Rp466 the shares are at 0.8x book and 4.2x our FY2026E EBITDA, with a possible refund of duties already paid carried at a probability weight as our own estimate and the first dividend since FY2022 declared [S10][S3].
The bear case is real: a quarter-weight scenario values the equity at Rp214 if the ex-duty spread returns to the FY2024 level and the frozen inventory needs a write-down [S8].

blocks.text: **BUY · target Rp739 · 62.4% expected return.** We initiate coverage of PT Sekar Bumi with a BUY rating and a twelve-month target of Rp739 against a share price of Rp466. With the declared interim dividend of Rp17.5 the expected return is 62.4%. The target is built from the probability-weighted scenario value of Rp924, carried forward at the 14.8% cost of equity and cut by a 20.0% liquidity discount for a company whose free float is 14.7% of the register [S3]. Our primary method is a discounted cash flow at an 11.6% WACC, which values the equity at Rp703 a share; the P/E cross-check sits well below it and the EV/EBITDA cross-check above it, for identifiable reasons we take apart in section four [S10][S3].

The variant view is the duty line's mechanics, not its direction. The market reads the US anti-dumping and reciprocal-tariff charge as a permanent margin tax; the filings show it is passed through and grossed up, and it is still rising — IDR360.1bn in 9M2026 against IDR243.0bn in 9M2025, up sharply and already above the whole of FY2025's IDR312.6bn [S4][S5]. Because the LK states that the tariff was effectively passed on to customers and that the higher selling price accounted for duties and tariffs, the charge increases revenue and selling expenses together [S3]. So the duty level is not what determines profitability: strip it from both sides and the ex-duty gross margin widened from the FY2024 trough to a FY2025 peak and eased only modestly in 9M2026. That is the series to underwrite. What is unvalued is the refund route the Supreme Court's annulment of the earlier IEEPA schedule opened: the annual report says the decision opened the way for potential refunds, but the company discloses no claim, amount or timetable, so we carry our own probability-weighted estimate in the bridge rather than a company promise [S3].

The recovery is already visible in the accounts rather than being a forecast. Nine-month FY2026 sales were IDR2,811.9bn, gross profit IDR732.9bn and net profit attributable to owners IDR120.2bn, against a much weaker comparable period [S4]. The company entered FY2024 with a gross margin of 13.7% and a loss at the net line, then rebuilt to a 25.7% gross margin in FY2025 on sales of IDR3,013.7bn [S5][S4]. Part of that step is the duty gross-up and part is a genuine widening of the product spread; the ex-duty arithmetic in section three separates the two, and the genuine part is what the forecast is built on.

What the price discounts is the opposite. At Rp466 the shares trade at 0.8x book value and 4.2x our FY2026E EBITDA, with a trailing P/E of 11.6x that is inflated by a duty-depressed earnings base [S0]. If the ex-duty spread fell back to the FY2024 level and stayed there, the equity would be worth the bear-case value in section five; if the 9M2026 spread holds, it is worth substantially more. That binary is the investment case, and it is why the target is not a smooth extrapolation.

Three things move the value. First, whether the ex-duty spread holds near its 9M2026 level as farm-gate shrimp prices normalise [S4]. Second, whether the duty refund route converts: the annual report says the Supreme Court decision opened the way for potential refunds, and we carry our own estimate of half the duties booked in FY2025 and 9M2026 at a probability below even odds, worth a material addition to the bridge [S3]. Third, whether the receivables that ballooned during the FDA import-alert period unwind: trade receivables reached IDR615.6bn at the September balance-sheet date and are the single largest use of cash in the model [S4].

We are explicit about the other side. A quarter-weight bear case values the equity at Rp214, because the same trade file that can clear can also re-close, and because a processor with a thin free float and all of its bank debt in short-term facilities has limited room to absorb a second shock [S8][S4]. A reader who thinks the US tariff regime is structurally hostile to Indonesian shrimp should own the bear case, not this note.
What Sekar Bumi is

PT Sekar Bumi was established in April 1973 and has been listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 1992; the annual report describes it as a pioneer of frozen shrimp processing in the country [S3]. It is a manufacturer, not a farmer or a trader: it buys and contracts raw shrimp and other seafood, processes it in certified plants, freezes it and sells it to overseas food-service and retail customers and to the Indonesian market. That distinction matters for the economics, because the company sits between a volatile, fragmented farm-gate supply base and concentrated Western buyers, and its margin is the spread between the two plus whatever its value-added preparation earns.
Products, brands and mix

The product set has two reported legs. Under value-added seafood the company produces prepared shrimp, fish, squid and other seafood; under processed food it makes dim sum, fish balls, breaded shrimp and sausages. It also produces shrimp and fish feed and cashew nuts, which are small relative to the seafood business [S3]. Brands are FINNA and SKB for the export seafood range, Bumifood for the domestic and ready-to-eat range, and Mitraku for the feed and cashew activities [S3].

The mix is unusually concentrated in one leg. Value-added seafood was 89.9% of FY2025 sales and processed food 10.1%, so the investment case is the shrimp-export case and very little else [S8]. Within value-added seafood, the annual report describes frozen value-added seafood as the largest contributor to export sales [S3]. The company has been shifting further into prepared and ready-to-eat formats — its Quick Bites line under Bumifood is described as the first ready-to-eat seafood product in the country — because prepared products carry a wider spread than commodity frozen shrimp [S3].
Footprint, volumes and customers

Sales are overwhelmingly external. Exports were 91.0% of FY2025 revenue, equivalent to the great majority of the top line, with the domestic market making up the remainder [S3]. The destination list is broad for a company of this size: the United States is the largest single market, with Europe, Australia, Japan, South Korea, China and other Asian countries alongside it, and the public expose maps customers across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific [S3][S8]. Domestic sales run through food service, general trade and modern trade, with a factory and distribution base in Java [S8].

Volumes are disclosed by product line rather than by customer. FY2025 production of value-added seafood was 21,153 t tonnes, up sharply on the prior year, and processed food production was 5,810 t tonnes [S3]. Those tonnages against revenue of IDR3,013.7bn imply a high revenue per tonne, which is consistent with prepared shrimp rather than bulk frozen commodity. The company does not disclose customer concentration; we treat that as an evidence gap rather than assuming either a concentrated or a diversified book [S3].
Group structure and ownership

The group is a set of largely wholly owned operating companies under common management control: PT Bumi Pangan Asri, PT Bumi Pangan Utama, PT Sekar Bumi Industri, PT Bumi Pangan Sejahtera, PT Sekar Bumi Distrindo, PT Bumifood Agro Industri, PT Sekar Katokichi and PT Sentra Budidaya Biotek, several of which are not commercially operational or are affiliates [S3][S8]. The minority interests that remain are small and were loss-making in the latest period, which is why the model carries no minority share of profit [S4].

Control is concentrated. TAEL Two Partners Ltd holds 32.1% and Green Resources Investments Pte. Ltd. 19.6%, with the board and remaining holders making up the balance; the data pack puts insider ownership at 75.3% and the free float at 14.7% [S3][S0]. The president commissioner is Finna Huang and the president director is Oei Harry Lukmito, with Howard Ken Lukmito as vice president director — a family-linked board of the kind common in Indonesian mid-caps [S3]. The consequences for minority holders are discussed in section six.
Strategy and competitive position

Management's stated strategy is to push further into value-added and ready-to-eat products, defend and deepen the existing export markets of Japan, Australia and China, and grow the domestic business through Bumifood [S3]. Capital intensity is low: the asset base is already built, FY2025 capex was IDR30.4bn against depreciation of IDR32.5bn, and the public expose announced no new plant [S8][S5]. The company targets sales of IDR4,000.0bn in FY2026, a plan our model does not fully adopt because it assumes a faster duty normalisation than the accounts currently show [S3].

Competitively, Sekar Bumi is a long-established specialist rather than a scale leader. The annual report calls it a pioneer, but it does not claim a market share, and the global shrimp-processing industry is fragmented across Indonesia, India, Ecuador and Vietnam [S3]. Its real assets are its certifications, its customer relationships in the US and Japan, and its product development; its weakness is that it is a price-taker on both sides of the spread, with no control over farm-gate shrimp or over US tariff policy [S3]. The company employs 837.0 people, which is small for a business with this revenue base and reflects the labour-light, capital-light nature of freezing and packing [S0].
The trade the company is in

Sekar Bumi competes in the global frozen-shrimp trade, where the United States is the demand centre and a handful of low-cost aquaculture producers — Ecuador, India, Vietnam and Indonesia — are the supply base [S3]. The annual report records that Ecuador became the largest exporter of shrimp to the United States in 2025, overtaking India, Indonesia and Vietnam, on the back of a lower tariff and rapid pond expansion [S3]. That is the structural backdrop: this is a commodity-protein trade with differentiated preparation at the margin, not a branded-consumer category with pricing power.

The addressable market is not disclosed in any of the company's filings, and no Indonesian industry body statistic in the archive sizes the frozen-shrimp export pool [S3]. We therefore do not put a market-size number in this report. What the company does disclose is enough to establish the mechanics: export sales grew from the prior year to the majority of revenue on higher volumes and prices that already included the duty, and the domestic market grew more slowly [S3].
Tariffs are the industry's swing factor

The US tariff file has moved repeatedly and each move reset relative competitiveness. In April 2025 the United States set a base tariff plus a much higher special rate for Indonesia; the special rate was cut and the combined rate settled at 19.0% from August 2025 under the reciprocal agreement [S8]. Anti-dumping duties are separate and were set at a final rate of 3.9% [S8]. In February 2026 the US Supreme Court annulled the earlier IEEPA-based tariffs and the administration substituted a lower global tariff [S8]; the annual report says the decision opened the way for potential refunds of duties already paid, without quantifying a claim [S3].

Relative to competitors, Indonesia's position improved rather than deteriorated. India faced a tariff of 50.0%, Ecuador 15.0% and Vietnam a little above that, so Indonesian product was mid-pack and clearly better placed than Indian supply [S3]. The company makes the point explicitly: because the tariff is passed on to customers, the rate affects competitiveness and volume rather than the margin line [S3]. That claim is central to our model and we test it in the scenarios — if it is wrong, the duty becomes a margin tax and the bear case is the right one.
The FDA is the second regulator

In August 2025 the US Food and Drug Administration detected radioactive caesium in frozen shrimp from an Indonesian exporter, and shrimp from Java and Lampung was placed under a US import alert on shrimp from Java and Lampung [S8]; every US-bound shrimp shipment from those regions now needs an additional radioactivity-free certificate issued by the Indonesian fisheries quality agency [S8]. The company discloses that the tighter testing disrupted its business cycle and cash flow and lengthened receivables collection [S3]. Both of its Java plants sit inside the affected geography, so this is a direct constraint rather than a sector curiosity [S3][S8].
Competitive landscape and five forces

Supplier power is high and volatile: raw shrimp comes from fragmented farmers and collectors whose prices move with the global pond cycle, and the company hedges none of it [S3]. Buyer power is high: US food-service and retail customers are large, certification-driven and able to switch origin within a season. The threat of new entrants is moderated by certification and customer audits but not eliminated, since processing capacity in Vietnam and Ecuador is easy to add relative to brand building. Substitutes are other origins rather than other proteins, which is why tariff differentials move volume so sharply. Rivalry is fragmented and price-based, with Ecuador the current low-cost benchmark [S3].

The moat is therefore thin but not absent. Sekar Bumi has decades-old customer relationships, internationally certified plants and a product-development capability that lets it sell prepared shrimp rather than blocks of frozen commodity; the annual report leans on certification and quality rather than on scale or cost leadership [S3]. We would not pay a franchise multiple for this business, which is why the DCF carries a mid-teens cost of equity rather than a consumer-staples one.

Shrimp aquaculture is a biological production system with a short cycle, so supply responds to price within a year and farm-gate prices can swing sharply. Processors who own no ponds sit between that cycle and Western retail buyers, and their margins compress when pond prices rise and buyers resist re-pricing. Certification regimes in importing countries are the main non-price barrier, and they can be withdrawn quickly after a contamination event.
External influences

The macro deck drives the valuation only indirectly. Revenue is dollar-denominated while most costs are rupiah, so the rupiah level matters: the deck has USD/IDR at Rp18,063/USD spot and Rp17,570/USD for FY2026, a weaker rupiah than the FY2025 average of Rp16,448/USD, which flatters translated revenue [S0]. Indonesian policy rates set the floor under the company's short-term bank cost, and US demand conditions set the volume. No deck series prices shrimp, so the model carries margin directly rather than through a fabricated commodity link — the reasons are set out in section three and section four [S3].
Four years of tariff cycle, not a growth series

The reported history is best read as one trade shock followed by a partial recovery. Revenue was IDR3,802.3bn in FY2022, fell to IDR2,839.6bn and then IDR2,269.4bn as the US trade file deteriorated, and recovered to IDR3,013.7bn in FY2025 — still below the FY2022 level [S5][S8]. The company is not a compounder that had a bad year; it is a cyclical exporter that has just regained most of its former top line, with the FY2026 run-rate now above it on our numbers.

Margins tell the same story with more force. Gross margin was 16.1% in FY2022, 12.1% in FY2023 and 13.7% in FY2024 before jumping to 25.7% in FY2025 [S5]. EBITDA margin went from 3.9% to -1.9% and back to 5.7%, and net profit attributable to owners went from IDR86.2bn to a loss of IDR-75.2bn and back to IDR69.5bn [S5]. The swing is not a volume story; it is the combination of the duty charge, the shrimp input price and the product mix shifting toward prepared seafood.
The duty line is still rising, and it is a gross-up

FY2025 revenue grew 32.8% on the prior year, and the company attributes the growth to higher export volumes and prices that had been adjusted for the duty [S3]. The duty inside selling expenses rose from IDR54.9bn in FY2024 to IDR312.6bn in FY2025 [S3]. That is not the end of the cycle: The selling-expense note of the 9M2026 LK shows IDR360.1bn of duties and tariffs against IDR243.0bn in 9M2025, up sharply and already above the whole of FY2025 [S4]. The line therefore scales with the US shipment value rather than with a rate that is falling, and we model it that way.

The accounting consequences are what matter. SG&A in FY2025 was IDR486.5bn of selling expenses plus IDR164.8bn of G&A, and the audited operating profit was IDR140.5bn, which with the restated D&A charge gives the EBITDA the multiples in section four use [S5]. The reported gross profit of IDR774.4bn carries the duty on both sides of the ratio, because the selling price charged to US customers includes it [S3]. Stripping the duty from revenue and from gross profit gives the ex-duty margin series below; this is the comparable series, and the model's gross-margin line is calibrated to it rather than to the reported percentage.
The duty line was IDR54.9bn on revenue of IDR2,269.4bn in FY2024, IDR312.6bn on IDR3,013.7bn in FY2025 and IDR360.1bn on IDR2,811.9bn in the first nine months of FY2026 [S3][S4].

The duty ratio is the reason the reported margin is not comparable across years: it rose from a low single-digit share of revenue in FY2024 to a tenth of revenue in FY2025 and to more than that in 9M2026 [S3][S4]. A rising duty ratio mechanically lifts the reported gross margin even if the product spread is unchanged, because the duty is charged inside the selling price and so is carried in both revenue and gross profit, with the matching cost in selling expenses [F8][F36][F40]. The ex-duty series therefore removes the duty from both sides of the gross-margin fraction: for FY2025, IDR774.4bn of gross profit less IDR312.6bn of duty, over IDR3,013.7bn of revenue less the same duty; the same construction on the FY2024 and 9M2026 lines gives the three periods we anchor the terminal margin on. The operating line needs no such adjustment — the duty surplus in gross profit is exactly offset in selling expenses — so the ex-duty operating margin is IDR140.5bn over revenue less the duty, and that is the level the terminal year reproduces. This is why we underwrite the ex-duty series and why the scenario shocks in section five are applied to it.

Inventories are the other quality issue. The inventory note shows the net-realisation provision falling from IDR18.0bn at 31 December 2024 to IDR1.9bn at 31 December 2025, after the FY2025 write-off, and IDR419.6bn of frozen stock remained at 30 September 2026 [S4]. Frozen shrimp is perishable and re-prices with the global pond cycle, so a fresh write-down is a live risk rather than a historical one; we carry it in the bear case and watch the provision at each balance-sheet date.

The company's own summary of the year shows the operating leverage in the recovery: gross profit roughly doubled while selling expense grew faster than sales, and general and administrative cost grew only modestly [S8]. That is the signature of a duty gross-up passing through the top line rather than a structural cost increase, and it is why we model the opex ratio falling as the rate normalises rather than assuming the FY2025 ratio persists.
The D&A restatement

The data pack's depreciation line was a fraction of the real charge, so we restated it from the audited FY2025 accounts. The fixed-asset note in the FY2025 LK shows fixed-asset depreciation of IDR32.5bn charged in FY2025 (split between cost of goods sold and administrative expense) and IDR30.8bn in FY2024 [S5]. The pack carried only a small share of that, which understated EBITDA and overstated the EBITDA multiple, and it also flattered the capex-to-depreciation ratio. We keyed the note's figures into the model as facts and the engine restated the history; FY2025 EBITDA is now IDR173.0bn against the un-restated figure the pack implied.

The restatement does not change net profit, cash flow or equity — depreciation is non-cash and the audited income statement already deducted it — but it matters for three things. It lifts EBITDA and therefore lowers net debt to EBITDA to 1.9 in FY2025 and 1.1 in FY2026E. It makes the EV/EBITDA cross-check in section four more demanding, because the denominator is larger. And it reveals that capex of IDR30.4bn is running below depreciation, so the asset base is being consumed faster than it is renewed — fine for a company with no growth capex, a slow erosion if volumes keep rising [S5].
Nine-month FY2026 and our forecast

The nine-month accounts are the strongest evidence in the file. Sales of IDR2,811.9bn were up sharply on the comparable period, gross profit was IDR732.9bn and net profit attributable to owners was IDR120.2bn [S4]. Nine-month profit is already close to our full-year FY2026E forecast of IDR131.6bn, which tells us the forecast is conservative on the run-rate and that the fourth quarter carries the risk — year-end duty true-ups, a seasonal working-capital build and the unquantified warehouse fire [S9].

Our FY2026E build is deliberately below the company's plan. We forecast revenue of IDR3,706.8bn, growth of 23.0%, against management's target of IDR4,000.0bn [S3]. The gap is not scepticism about demand; it is that we do not assume the duty line disappears in the second half, only that it settles at the lower rate already being paid. Gross margin is held at 25.8%, close to the FY2025 actual. The opex ratio is the line that needs care, and its driver is not the duty charge: duty was IDR312.6bn in FY2025 and IDR360.1bn in 9M2026, so it is larger, not smaller [S3][S4]. The fall in the forecast ratio comes entirely from non-duty SG&A. FY2025 selling expenses of IDR486.5bn carried IDR312.6bn of duty, with G&A of IDR164.8bn [S5]; 9M2026 selling expenses of IDR432.3bn carried IDR360.1bn of duty, with G&A of IDR123.5bn [S4]. The non-duty ratio therefore dropped between the two periods even as the duty ratio rose. That drop embeds a fourth-quarter 2025 step-up in non-duty SG&A that we cannot tie to a disclosed one-off — we treat it as an unexplained true-up rather than a run-rate — so the FY2026E ratio is an extrapolation of the 9M2026 run-rate, not of FY2025. That produces EBITDA of IDR266.2bn, a 7.2% margin, and EPS of 76.1 [S4][S8].

Beyond FY2026 the model fades growth to 12.0% and then 8.0%, with gross margin drifting from 25.4% to 25.0% as shrimp input costs normalise from their current low level [S4]. EBITDA reaches IDR308.5bn and net profit IDR157.5bn. We do not model a second leg of growth from the domestic ready-to-eat launch, because the company discloses no volume or margin for it yet [S3].
Cash flow, working capital and the balance sheet

The cash flow is the weak point of the otherwise good FY2025 story. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR-52.4bn despite positive EBITDA, because operating working capital absorbed IDR155.5bn — the receivables build during the FDA alert and the inventory carried against longer shipment cycles [S4]. That reverses as the build unwinds: our model has free cash flow of IDR67.4bn in FY2026E and IDR72.6bn in FY2027E, with the working-capital ratio held at the September level rather than the FY2025 peak [S4].

The balance sheet is liquid but not comfortable. At the September date the company held IDR337.3bn of cash against IDR594.2bn of short-term bank loans; net debt was IDR321.5bn at the FY2025 close and is forecast at IDR292.7bn at the FY2026E close [S4]. Essentially all of the bank debt is short-term working-capital facilities, which is normal for an exporter but leaves no maturity cushion if a lender pulls a line. Goodwill of IDR195.0bn sits on the balance sheet from the Bumifood and Sekar Katokichi acquisitions and is a meaningful share of total assets; it is not at risk in our base case but it is the first thing to impair if the processed-food subsidiary misses [S4].

Capital allocation is conservative and now shareholder-friendly. Capex is maintenance-level, no acquisition or rights issue has been announced, and the company declared an interim dividend of Rp17.5 per share, IDR30.3bn in total, its first distribution since FY2022 [S10]. We model a payout ratio in line with the interim payment, which is the policy the company is now demonstrating rather than a historical average [S10].
Earnings quality

We cannot compute a clean accruals ratio from the archive: the model carries free cash flow but not a full cash-flow-from-operations line, and the pack's direct-method statement is unreliable. We treat that as an evidence gap and rely on the components instead. The receivables divergence is the clearest flag: trade receivables reached IDR615.6bn at the September date, after a FY2025 jump that ran at more than twice the sales growth rate, a classic sign of earnings outrunning collection, and they have partly unwound since [S4][S3]. We would want to see the FY2026 audited cash flow before concluding the flag is closed.

Three further checks are clean or explained. Related-party balances are immaterial — receivables and payables with affiliates are rounding errors against revenue — so the modal Indonesian value-destruction channel is not present at scale [S5]. No special-monitoring board status or special notation is disclosed, and the free float is small but the shares trade daily [S0]. The pack's understated depreciation is a data defect we have corrected, not a company disclosure problem [S5]. The one unresolved item is the unquantified warehouse fire, which we carry at zero because the company says operations were not stopped and has not booked a loss [S9].
Why this method set fits

We weight a discounted cash flow at 70% because Sekar Bumi's reported earnings are the wrong denominator for a multiple. The business is asset-light, cash conversion is driven by working capital rather than by capital investment, and the reported margin is a duty gross-up rather than a product spread, so a free-cash-flow model captures the economics better than an earnings multiple does [S5]. The earnings are distorted twice over: the duty sits in revenue and selling expenses, and the pack's depreciation was understated until we restated it [S3][S5]. A P/E on those earnings tells you more about the tariff than about the company, which is why we cut that method to 10% of the blend.

We keep the two multiple cross-checks at 10% and 20% because they are the way an Indonesian mid-cap investor will actually look at the name, and because a DCF with a large terminal-value share needs a reality check. The P/E is the smallest weight precisely because the engine applies it to last-twelve-month earnings per share of 40.2, the duty-depressed base we have just disowned; at a 10% weight an over-conservative method moves the blend by a few percent, not by fifteen. We do not use a book-value method: the shares trade at 0.8x book, but book includes IDR195.0bn of goodwill and a revalued asset base, so it is not a clean asset floor [S4].
Cost of capital

The cost of equity is 14.8% and the WACC is 11.6%. The build starts from a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, deducts the sovereign default spread of 1.6% so the same sovereign risk is not charged twice, and then adds the levered beta of 1.34 multiplied by the combined premium — the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5% [S0]. The beta multiplies the sum, not the mature premium alone: 1.34 × (4.2% + 2.5%) added to 7.4% less 1.6% is what produces 14.8%. The house band for rupiah discount rates is eleven to thirteen per cent, and our cost of equity sits one point eight percentage points above the top of it. The excess has one cause: country risk, levered. The 2.5% country premium is multiplied by the 1.34 beta rather than added once, which is the only reason the build clears the band; we add no small-cap premium (0.0% of extra premium). The unlevered beta is 0.85; it is a company parameter rather than a regression estimate, which we flag as thin evidence — a regression on this illiquid a line would not be reliable either. Leverage is the market-value D/E of 0.74, and the cost of debt is 9.4% pre-tax against a 22.0% tax rate [S4]. Weights are 57.6% equity and 42.4% debt. The only illiquidity charge is the 20.0% discount applied to the equity value, and it prices a different risk from the cost-of-equity excess: tradability — a 14.7% free float and IDR100.4m of daily turnover — rather than operating risk. The discount and the above-band cost of equity are therefore not two charges for the same thing.
Discounted cash flow

The DCF values the enterprise at IDR1,373.3bn and the equity at Rp703 a share, with the terminal value contributing 51.9% of the total. Two adjustments answer the obvious challenges. First, the terminal gross margin is faded, not held: it falls from 25.8% in FY2026 to the terminal-year rate set out in the assumptions, with the fade completed by FY2030, because the reported margin carries the duty gross-up and the ex-duty spread should normalise toward its three-period average rather than hold the FY2025 peak. Second, the terminal EBIT margin is unchanged by that fade because the operating-cost ratio is faded in step — a lower duty share lowers revenue, gross profit and selling expense together. Third, capex is split: maintenance is set at the restated D&A charge and growth capex is added on top, so total capex rises from the FY2025 level of a little over one percent of sales toward one and a half percent by FY2028, because the 9M2026 volume recovery ran on capacity installed before the trough, not on free capacity forever [S5]. Working capital is held at the September ratio and terminal growth is 4.0% — below Indonesian long-run nominal GDP, which the macro deck puts at real growth of 5.3% plus inflation of 3.3% [S0].
Growth, reinvestment and the multiple-survival test

Growth is manufactured, not declared, and here it is not worth much. The forecast reinvests IDR58.1bn of capex and IDR97.9bn of working capital against IDR44.8bn of D&A and IDR244.9bn of EBIT, a reinvestment rate of about three-fifths of NOPAT, and the incremental return on that capital is about seven per cent, below the 11.6% WACC: the terminal-year ROE is 8.5% against a 14.8% cost of equity [S0]. Beyond the fade, additional growth therefore destroys value, which is why the twelve-month sensitivity grid shows value falling as revenue growth rises. We are not paying for volume; the thesis is a margin call, and the spread is the only driver that earns its cost of capital.

The multiple-survival test points the same way. At the target, the equity value plus FY2026E net debt of IDR292.7bn, over FY2027E EBITDA of IDR289.8bn, implies an EV/EBITDA above the 4.2x at which the shares trade today — multiple expansion, not cash flow alone. A buyer at that exit multiple would be capitalising the margin recovery we have already assumed, with no further growth premium; that is a demanding ask for a processor whose terminal ROE is below its cost of equity. The target is therefore a probability-weighted scenario value, not a DCF exit multiple we would defend as fair.
Cross-checks and why they diverge

The P/E method gives Rp404, -42.4% relative to the DCF of Rp703, and the reason is mechanical rather than a disagreement about the business. The method applies a peer median multiple of 10.1x to last-twelve-month earnings per share of 40.2, a year in which the duty charge of IDR312.6bn sat in selling expenses and net profit was IDR69.5bn [S3]. That is not a normalised earnings base, so we do not give the method the weight the industry default would: it is 10% of the blend, and the DCF and EV/EBITDA methods carry the rest. Applied to our FY2026E EPS of 76.1, the same multiple would produce a value close to the EV/EBITDA cross-check; the gap between Rp404 and Rp734 is therefore the duty-depressed denominator, not a signal about the business.

The EV/EBITDA method gives Rp734, a 4.4% premium to the DCF of Rp703 — above it, not below. The method applies 8.2x, an average of the peer median and the company's own five-year average, to an EV that starts from the market capitalisation of IDR806.2bn and deducts the same 30 September 2026 balance sheet the DCF uses — IDR594.2bn of bank loans less IDR337.3bn of cash — rolled forward to the FY2026E close that supplies the EBITDA denominator; the DCF, by contrast, deducts the September net debt directly [S4]. A cross-check above the primary is not the comfort a below-primary check would be. Because the EV/EBITDA method starts from today's market price, it is partly circular: it tells us the market would capitalise our forward EBITDA at a higher value than our cash flows justify, not that an independent buyer would. It remains the cross-check closest to how an investor will look at the name, because it uses the restated EBITDA of IDR173.0bn and a multiple anchored on the company's own trading history, which is why we keep its weight at 20%; but we do not treat it as a second valuation. The P/E sits far below for the opposite reason — a duty-depressed earnings denominator — so the two multiples do not bracket the DCF. The DCF sits between them, and that is a reason to keep the DCF as the primary method rather than independent proof that the shares are cheap.
Sensitivity

The DCF grid moves value across WACC and terminal growth by one percentage point in each direction. Every cell in it is above the current share price, including the corner where the WACC is highest and terminal growth lowest [S0]. The one-year value grid, which shocks revenue growth and gross margin together, is more informative: a two-percentage-point cut in gross margin with slower growth takes the value toward the current price, and a larger margin shock takes it below. That is the honest map of the risk — this is a margin call, not a growth call.
What the price implies

We tried to solve the reverse DCF — what growth rate would justify Rp466 — and the engine could not bracket the price: even punitive growth assumptions leave the discounted value above the market price [S0]. That result is itself the answer. The market is not discounting slower growth; it is discounting either a permanently lower margin or a much higher required return than we think is warranted. To get from our cash flows to today's price, gross margin would have to revert toward the FY2024 level of 13.7% and stay there, with the duty line persisting at its peak, or the discount rate would have to rise far beyond anything the risk-free rate and country premium support.

That is what makes the expected return 62.4% rather than a modest premium. Three sourced drivers produce it. The first is the duty line: IDR312.6bn of anti-dumping and reciprocal tariff was charged in FY2025, the reciprocal rate fell to 19.0%, and the Supreme Court annulled the earlier schedule; the annual report says that decision opened the way for potential refunds, though no claim or amount is disclosed [S8][S3]. The second is realised margin: nine-month FY2026 gross profit of IDR732.9bn on sales of IDR2,811.9bn is an actual result, not a forecast [S4]. The third is the starting valuation: 0.8x book and 4.2x forward EBITDA, with the bear case at a quarter weight cutting the value by more than half, so the target is not a single-path extrapolation [S0][S8].

The bridge from enterprise to equity value deducts net debt and minorities and adds the probability-weighted refund [S4][S3]. Net debt is the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, not the 30 June data-pack figure: IDR594.2bn of short-term bank loans against IDR337.3bn of cash, with the small long-term and lease lines noted in section three, and minority interests of IDR16.8bn [S4]. That is a materially higher net debt than the mid-year pack carried, and the target reflects it — the earlier bridge understated the deduction and is withdrawn. The interim dividend is not deducted from value: it was declared on 9 November 2026, after the balance-sheet date, and the recording date is 20 November 2026, so a buyer today settles before the record date and receives it [S10][S2]. We therefore leave the IDR30.3bn inside equity value and add the same declared Rp17.5 to the expected return, rather than deducting it from value and adding it back. The duty refund is carried as a probability-weighted bridge item, but as our own estimate rather than a company claim: the annual report says the Supreme Court decision opened the way for potential refunds, while disclosing no claim, amount or timetable, so we take half of the duties booked in FY2025 and 9M2026, after tax, at a probability below even odds [S3]. Raising the probability to even would add a large amount per share and is the single biggest upside to the target. The liquidity discount of 20.0% applied to the probability-weighted scenario value reflects a free float of 14.7% and daily turnover of IDR100.4m, and it is the only small-cap adjustment in the model: the cost of equity is a mechanical build from the risk-free rate, the country risk premium and the levered beta, with no additional size premium added on top, so the two are not double-counting the same illiquidity [S0].
The risk map

This is a single-driver equity: almost everything that can hurt the share price runs through the US trade file or the shrimp input price. We rank the risks below by likelihood and impact, and we distinguish the ones we can source from the ones we can only flag.

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Why it matters | |---|---|---|---| | US tariff re-escalation | Medium | High | The reciprocal rate could be raised again; the refund route is not yet cash [S3][S8] | | FDA import alert widens or persists | Medium | High | Java and Lampung shipments need extra certification; collection cycles lengthen [S8][S3] | | Shrimp input cost normalises upward | Medium | High | The 25.8% margin is a spread, not a franchise [S3] | | Rupiah strength | Medium | Medium | Export revenue is dollar-denominated, costs are rupiah [S0] | | Refinancing of short-term bank lines | Low | High | Essentially all bank debt is short-term working capital [S4] | | Warehouse fire or food-safety event | Low | Medium | The September fire is not yet quantified [S9] | | Governance or related-party action | Low | Medium | Concentrated control, thin float [S3] |
Tariff risk is two-sided

The base case assumes the duty line stays where it is currently being paid, not that it disappears. The risk to that assumption runs both ways, and the upside is as relevant as the downside: the February 2026 Supreme Court decision annulled the earlier IEEPA tariffs, and the annual report says the decision opened the way for potential refunds, though no claim or amount is disclosed [S3]. If refunds are paid, the FY2026 or FY2027 accounts could carry a one-off credit beyond the estimate we carry. If instead the reciprocal rate is re-raised or the global tariff is increased, the duty line grows again and the bear case applies. The company's claim that it passes the tariff to customers is the single most important assertion in this report; it is sourced to management, not independently verified, and we treat a failure of that pass-through as the trigger for the bear case [S3].
The FDA constraint

The import alert covering shrimp from Java and Lampung is the second regulatory risk and it is more operational than the tariff [S8]. Extra per-shipment certification slows the cycle, lengthens receivables and raises the working-capital burden exactly when the company is trying to convert profit into cash [S3]. The company discloses no timeline for the alert's removal and no cost estimate; the public expose names the certifying agency but not a remediation date [S8]. We model the working-capital drag as permanent at the September ratio, which is the cautious side of this specific risk.
The shrimp cycle and the margin

Our gross margin path is the most sensitive assumption in the model. The FY2024 trough margin of 13.7% and the FY2025 margin of 25.7% bracket a wide range, and the current level depends on farm-gate shrimp prices staying where they are [S3]. The company buys rather than farms, so a supply shock hits COGS directly, and its export prices are set in contracts that re-price with a lag. This is the classic processor squeeze, and it is why the scenario shocks hit gross margin as well as revenue.
Currency and funding

Revenue is earned in dollars and costs are mostly rupiah, so a stronger rupiah compresses translated revenue; the deck has USD/IDR at Rp18,063/USD spot against a FY2025 average of Rp16,448/USD, so the recent direction has been helpful rather than harmful [S0]. On funding, the company carries IDR594.2bn of short-term bank loans against IDR337.3bn of cash; the facilities are working-capital lines secured on receivables and inventory, and a lender withdrawal would force a receivable sale or an equity raise [S4]. We do not model either, but it is the tail risk that the liquidity discount partly prices.
Scenarios

The three scenarios shock the same drivers in mirrored directions and carry probabilities that sum to one. Base is the most probable path at 50.0%: the duty line stays at the current lower rate, gross margin holds near the nine-month actual, and working capital unwinds gradually, giving a value of Rp762.

Bear, at 25.0%, re-raises the reciprocal rate toward the level threatened in 2025 and widens the FDA alert beyond the current regions, so US volume is lost and the duty burden stays in selling expenses while the operating ratio rises as fixed costs are spread over lower volume and farm-gate shrimp prices recover, making the margin the peak of a soft raw-material cycle. It values the equity at Rp214.

Bull, at 25.0%, clears the trade file without the duty disappearing: the FDA alert is lifted on documented certification and US volume recovers, the ex-duty spread holds at the FY2025 peak rather than fading, and the non-duty SG&A ratio falls as the recovery spreads fixed costs while the duty line stays in selling expenses. A weak rupiah lifts IDR revenue per tonne while farm-gate shrimp stays cheap, with domestic food service adding a second leg. It values the equity at Rp1,959.

The probability-weighted value is Rp924, and after the 20.0% liquidity discount and the roll-forward at the cost of equity the target is Rp739. The scenarios are mirrored: each shocks the same three drivers by the same amount in the opposite direction, and the probabilities are symmetric at a quarter for each tail around a half-weight base. What is asymmetric is the payoff — the bull is worth well over twice the base and the bear a fraction of it — so the expected value, and the target, leans on the bull. That dependence is the main thing the red team should attack, and it is why the bull is written to the shocks actually applied, not to a duty elimination the company's own disclosure does not support.
Signposts that change the view

We would cut the rating if the quarterly selling-expense line shows the duty charge rising again as a share of sales, if the FDA alert is extended to additional provinces, or if gross margin falls below the FY2024 level for two consecutive quarters [S3][S8]. We would raise the target if a refund is actually received, if the alert is lifted with a documented certification path, or if the company discloses customer or volume data that confirms the mix shift into prepared seafood is durable [S3]. The single cleanest signpost is the FY2026 audited cash flow statement: it will tell us whether the receivables build was a tariff-timing artefact or a permanent change in collection terms [S4].
Ownership and control

Control sits with two external holders and the board. TAEL Two Partners Ltd owns 32.1% and Green Resources Investments Pte. Ltd. 19.6%; the directors and commissioners hold the balance of the insider block, and the data pack puts total insider ownership at 75.3% with a free float of 14.7% [S3][S0]. That is a controlled company by any standard: a minority shareholder cannot outvote the block, and the practical protection is the dividend and the disclosure record rather than the ballot.

The board is family-linked. Finna Huang is president commissioner, Oei Harry Lukmito is president director, Howard Ken Lukmito is vice president director, and Gary Iyawan, Freddy Adam and Pahlawan Hari Tjahjono complete the directorate [S3]. We found no evidence of a professional independent majority, and the annual report does not disclose a share pledge by the controlling holders — an absence of disclosure rather than a clean bill of health, and a point the red team should test [S3].
Related parties and group structure

The group operates through a set of subsidiaries under common management control, several of which are dormant or affiliates [S3][S8]. Related-party trade, however, is immaterial to the accounts: trade receivables from related parties were IDR0.4bn at the FY2025 close, and related-party payables are of the same order [S5]. This matters because related-party gravity is the modal value-destruction channel on the Indonesia Stock Exchange, and here it is simply not present at a scale that could move earnings. We classify the structure as an optics flag — concentrated control and a family board — rather than a manipulation-class flag.

The subsidiary structure does carry one substantive risk: goodwill of IDR195.0bn from the Bumifood and Sekar Katokichi acquisitions sits on the balance sheet, and the non-controlling interests were loss-making in the latest period [S4]. If the processed-food subsidiary underperforms, impairment would hit book value and the P/B support that some investors rely on [S4].
Audit, disclosure and dividends

The FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Paul Hadiwinata, Hidajat, Arsono, Retno, Palilingan & Rekan, a mid-tier Indonesian firm, for a fee disclosed in the annual report [S3]. The archived auditor's report pages are image-only, so we could not verify the opinion wording ourselves; that is a thin-evidence point we are flagging rather than papering over [S3]. Disclosure quality is adequate but not generous: volumes are disclosed by product line, but customer concentration, capacity utilisation and the cost of the FDA remediation are not [S3][S8].

The dividend record is improving. The last full-year dividend, in FY2022, was Rp10.0 per share, nothing was paid in the following three years while the company rebuilt the balance sheet, and has now declared an interim dividend of Rp17.5 per share, IDR30.3bn in total, the first distribution since FY2022 [S10]. We read the reinstatement as a signal that management expects the cash conversion to normalise, and we hold them to it in the FY2026 audited accounts.
ESG exposures

The material ESG issues are food safety and marine sourcing, not carbon. The caesium detection that triggered the FDA import alert is a food-safety and reputation event that the company has not yet quantified, and the extra certification burden falls on its own plants [S8][S3]. Sourcing is the second exposure: the company buys from a fragmented farm base, so antibiotic residues, labour standards and traceability in the supply chain are the risks that could trigger another import restriction. The annual report describes internationally certified processing plants and a quality-control system, but discloses no quantified sustainability targets, no Scope emissions and no third-party audit of suppliers [S3]. We score ESG disclosure as weak and the exposure as real but manageable at current volumes.
Dated catalysts

The near-term calendar is dominated by the dividend and the trade file. The interim dividend of Rp17.5 per share has a 20 November 2026 recording date, with the distribution timetable to be announced — the first distribution since FY2022 and a concrete signal that the board believes the cash flow has normalised [S10][S2]. The company's next scheduled disclosure is the FY2026 audited result, expected in the first quarter of 2027, which will show whether the duty line stayed near the lower reciprocal rate through the second half [S4].

The unscheduled catalysts matter more. A refund of duties paid under the annulled IEEPA schedule would be a one-off credit; the model carries only a probability-weighted estimate of it, not a company-guided amount [S3]. A change in the FDA import-alert status for Java and Lampung would shorten the certification cycle and release working capital [S8]. A re-escalation of the reciprocal rate, or a widening of the alert, would push the shares toward the bear value [S8]. The annual public expose in mid-2027 is where management normally restates its sales target; this year's target of IDR4,000.0bn is above our forecast and we will test it against the FY2026 actual [S3].
The KPIs we watch

We monitor five lines between updates. First, selling expense as a share of sales, which is where the duty charge sits and the cleanest read on whether the tariff burden is rising or falling [S3]. Second, gross margin, which is the spread between farm-gate shrimp and export prices and the variable that drives the valuation [S4]. Third, trade receivables and their days outstanding, which tell us whether the FDA-related collection drag is temporary [S4]. Fourth, the split between export and domestic sales, because the domestic ready-to-eat launch is the only candidate second leg of growth and it is currently too small to disclose separately [S3]. Fifth, net debt to EBITDA and the maturity profile of the bank lines, given that essentially all the debt is short-term [S4].

We will revisit the rating on any of the following: a refund received; the import alert lifted; two consecutive quarters of gross margin below the FY2024 level; a re-acceleration of the duty charge; or a refinancing that converts short-term lines into term debt with covenants [S4][S3]. Absent those, the next scheduled review is the FY2026 audited result and the FY2027 public expose.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the 9M2026 actual: net sales Rp2,811.9bn, +29.7% on 9M2025, after FY2025's +32.8% recovery from the FY2024 tariff trough. Volume is production-led (value-added seafood +23.8% to 21,153t in FY2025) and price is USD export ASP, which carries the duty gross-up: the LK says export growth came from volume and from a selling price that accounted for duties and tariffs [S3]. FY2026 stays at the 9M2026 run-rate; FY2027 grows 12% toward the company's Rp4trn FY2026 target rather than decelerating against it, then fades to a 4.5% nominal terminal rate below Indonesian nominal GDP.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The reported margin is a duty gross-up, not a product spread. The duty is charged to customers inside the selling price and booked in selling expenses, so it lifts revenue, the gross-profit surplus and SG&A together and nets out in operating profit [F8/F36/F40]. Removing it from both revenue and the matching gross-profit surplus gives ex-duty gross margins of 11.6% in FY2024, 17.1% in FY2025 ((774.4 - 312.6) / (3,013.7 - 312.6)) and 15.2% in 9M2026 ((732.9 - 360.1) / (2,811.9 - 360.1)), an average of 14.6%. The terminal reported gross margin of 23.0%, with the duty assumed at 10% of revenue from FY2030, is an ex-duty gross margin of 14.4% ((0.230 - 0.10) / 0.90) - the three-period average, not a haircut below it. No moat justifies holding the FY2025 17.1% peak; the fade to FY2030 is the path to that sourced anchor.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: SG&A is dominated by the US trade-duty line, which sits in selling expenses: Rp54.9bn in FY2024, Rp312.6bn in FY2025 (10.4% of sales) and Rp360.1bn in 9M2026 (12.8%), so the line is still rising, not past its peak [F30/F31/F32]. SG&A was 21.6% of FY2025 revenue and 19.7% in 9M2026. The terminal ratio of 18.3% against the 23.0% terminal gross margin holds the reported operating margin at 4.7%, which is 5.2% of ex-duty revenue and reproduces the FY2025 audited operating margin on the same basis (operating profit Rp140.5bn over ex-duty revenue of Rp2,701.1bn) [F38/F40]. Because the duty is passed through and grossed up in revenue, the ratio is faded in step with the gross margin: a lower duty share lowers revenue, gross profit and selling expense together without changing operating profit.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from note 11 of the audited FY2025 LK: fixed-asset depreciation Rp32,497,811,173 (1.08% of sales), not the Rp10.37bn the data pack carries [S5, F3].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Split into maintenance and growth. Maintenance is set at the restated D&A charge of 1.08% of sales (Rp32.5bn in FY2025); growth capex starts at zero in FY2026 because the 29.7% 9M2026 volume recovery ran on spare capacity after the FY2024 trough - capex of Rp30.4bn was below D&A - and then builds to 0.4-0.45% of sales as the freezer and processing lines that support Rp4trn+ of sales are added. Total capex therefore rises from 1.2% of sales in FY2026 to 1.5% from FY2028, against the 1.1% assumed before. No new plant is announced [S8].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Receivables and inventory are the business: trade receivables Rp616.0bn plus inventory Rp419.6bn at 30 Sep 2026 against payables of Rp205.5bn. Held at 22% of revenue, slightly below the FY2025 23.7% because FY2025's 126% receivables jump (85 days vs 50 days in FY2024) unwound to 9M2026.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 tax charge implies ~25% on pre-tax profit; FY2025's 28.2% reflected non-deductible items. The statutory 22% plus a small permanent-difference add-on is what the filings show being paid [S4].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 interest and finance charges Rp38.5bn on average bank debt near Rp600bn, ~8.5%; the FY2025 ratio of 7.8% understates the 2026 rate after the rupiah moved to ~18,000/USD [S4].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 interest income Rp2.0bn on ~Rp337bn of cash is ~0.8% annualised; kept at 1.5% as the average of the last three years' cash yield.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new term debt announced; working-capital lines roll. Debt is held flat in nominal terms rather than assumed repaid, which is the conservative direction for equity value.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Other income is small and lumpy (FX gains and asset sales of Rp22.5bn in 9M2026); not forecast.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interest fell to Rp16.8bn at 30 Sep 2026 and absorbed a Rp1.0bn loss in 9M2026 after the subsidiary liquidation; modelled at zero rather than the FY2023-25 average, which is distorted by FY2024's loss [S4].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The 9 Nov 2026 interim dividend of Rp17.5/share (Rp30.3bn) is 23% of our FY2026E net profit, so FY2026 payout is set at 23% on the declared amount rather than a policy guess; 20% thereafter is the level the company is now demonstrating, not a historical average [S10].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 1,730,103,217 shares issued and fully paid, unchanged since the FY2020 ESOP; no rights issue or split announced [S10].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Below Indonesian long-run nominal GDP (real ~5.3%, CPI ~3.3% in the macro deck): a frozen-food exporter with a 0.8x book multiple does not compound at GDP forever.

challenges.challenge: The variant view - that FY2025 was the peak of the US duty charge - is contradicted by the report's own key source. Note 30 of the 9M2026 LK (S4) discloses Bea masuk dan tarif of Rp360,056,627,554 for 9M2026 against Rp242,953,359,625 for 9M2025, up 48% and already above FY2025's full-year Rp312.6bn [S4 vs F8/S3]. The report never cites the 9M duty line, and the 2026 selling-expense total reconciles only with that Rp360.1bn included.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt from the filings: the selling-expense note shows duties of Rp360.1bn in 9M2026 against Rp243.0bn in 9M2025, above FY2025's Rp312.6bn. The peak-duty framing is deleted and the pass-through gross-up is disclosed: the LK says the tariff was passed to customers and the selling price accounted for duties, so revenue carries the charge. New facts F30/F31 and F32; the growth story now runs on the ex-duty spread.

challenges.challenge: One passage states the duty rose from IDR312.6bn in the prior year to the level booked in FY2025, but S3 says it rose from Rp54.9bn in 2024 to Rp312.6bn in 2025. The quote does not say what the report claims and it inverts the direction the whole section depends on.
challenges.answer: Corrected to the LK's wording: duties rose from Rp54.9bn in FY2024 to Rp312.6bn in FY2025, not from Rp312.6bn to the FY2025 level. The sentence now matches the summary, the new F32 fact and the annual report quote.

challenges.challenge: The DCF capitalises a 24.5% terminal gross margin (terminal value is 50.4% of EV) against audited gross margins of 16.1%, 12.1% and 13.7% in FY2022-FY2024; only FY2025 exceeded 25%. The house card requires excess returns to fade unless a moat is named, and the report says the moat is thin. The bear shocks gross margin only 2pp.
challenges.answer: Terminal gross margin faded from 25.8% in FY2026 to 23.0% in FY2030 and held in the terminal year, with the operating-cost ratio faded in step so the terminal EBIT margin stays at the audited FY2025 level. The report now states the fade year and decomposes the reported margin into a duty gross-up and an ex-duty spread; the bear shock is widened to 3pp, mirrored by the bull, because the FY2024 13.7% is not comparable at a near-zero duty ratio.

challenges.challenge: Capex is held at 1.1% of sales, equal to depreciation, while revenue rises 62% to FY2035, so the model assumes 62% more output from the same asset base. The report notes FY2025 capex of Rp30.4bn ran below depreciation but never reconciles that with the growth path [S5].
challenges.answer: Capex is split explicitly: maintenance equals the restated D&A charge and growth capex is added on top, taking total capex from 1.2% of sales in FY2026 to 1.5% from FY2028. The text ties the FY2025-26 volume recovery to capacity installed before the trough, with FY2025 capex of Rp30.4bn below D&A of Rp32.5bn.

challenges.challenge: The P/E cross-check applies 10.1x to FY2025 EPS of 40.2 - the base the report itself calls abnormal - and keeps it at 30% weight, while stating that the same multiple on FY2026E EPS of 76.1 would give about Rp766. The blended 690 is therefore mechanically about 15% below the DCF for a reason the report has already disowned.
challenges.answer: The P/E method applies the peer multiple to LTM EPS from the duty-depressed FY2025 base the note disowns, so its weight is cut from 30% to 10% and redistributed to the DCF and EV/EBITDA, which use forward or operating earnings. The blend no longer carries a 15% mechanical drag from a mis-specified denominator; the change is justified in qc_justifications.weights.changed.
